transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Hi. Um… I guess what brings me in is these thoughts I keep having that I can’t shake. It’s like, if I miss one setting, one access rule, one warning sign—just one thing—then someone could get hurt, or lose everything, or some huge disaster could happen, and it would be my fault.

I know, at least part of me knows, that it’s not always rational. Like, I can hear myself saying it and I know it sounds extreme. But in the moment it doesn’t feel extreme—it feels urgent and completely real, like I’m personally responsible for preventing every possible bad outcome. And I can’t just move on from it the way other people seem to. It sort of grabs hold of me.
Can you tell me more about these thoughts? Specifically, do they involve any ideas about something harmful happening to you or someone else, like an accident, injury, or something aggressive?

Yes—well, not like I’m picturing myself attacking someone or anything like that. It’s more that I get stuck on the idea that if I miss something—some setting, some access rule, some alert or warning sign—then something really bad could happen to someone else. Like someone could be harmed, or lose everything, or there could be this cascading disaster because I failed to catch one detail.

And I know that sounds dramatic when I say it out loud. Part of me can see that the likelihood probably isn’t as high as it feels. But in the moment it hits me like it’s immediate and real, like I’m the one person standing between things being okay and something awful happening. I can’t just say, “I did enough,” and move on. My mind keeps circling back to, “What if you missed the one thing that matters?”

Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking things over and over, reviewing steps, or trying to neutralize the thoughts in some way—to try to reduce the anxiety or prevent the bad outcome from happening?

Yes. Yeah, I do. That’s actually a big part of why I’m here, I think, because it’s not just the thought—it’s what I end up doing afterward.

I’ll reread deployment plans over and over, like line by line, even if I already checked them. Then I’ll go back and compare them against audit logs, permissions, access rules, alerts… and I don’t just check once. I’ll think, “Okay, one more pass, just to make sure,” but then that pass doesn’t feel complete, so I start again. Sometimes I’ll count through the steps in my head, like I’m trying to make the sequence feel… safe, I guess. Like if I can mentally account for every possible step in the right order, then maybe I can let it go.

And it’s not only work systems. I’ll check door locks too, and sometimes old messages—like if I sent something or approved something, I’ll reread the wording again and again to make sure I didn’t miss some implication or instruction that could cause a problem later. I know it probably sounds excessive, but when I try to stop before it feels finished, I get this sharp panic, like I’m walking away from something dangerous.

There have been nights where I’ve stayed at the office for hours after everyone else left, just reviewing and rechecking. Not because there was necessarily an actual emergency, but because I couldn’t convince myself it was safe to stop.
Do these thoughts and checking behaviors happen every day, or do they come in waves where they feel more intense for a period of time and then maybe ease up a bit?

I’m… not completely sure how to answer that cleanly. It feels like it’s there so much that I don’t really have a good baseline to compare it to anymore, if that makes sense.

I mean, I can say there are definitely times when it feels more intense—like it ramps up and I get much more trapped in the checking—but I don’t know if I’ve tracked it well enough to say, “Yes, it’s daily,” or “No, it comes in waves.” I haven’t really kept a record of it. It’s more like I notice when I’m already deep in it, when I’ve lost a lot of time and I’m still not reassured.

Some days I can move through things a little more normally, or at least it looks that way from the outside, but then other times the same kind of thought just latches on and I can’t let it go. So… I guess I’d say it varies, but I’m not sure I can give you a precise pattern. It doesn’t feel random exactly, but I also haven’t been able to step back enough to map it out.
When you have these thoughts, do you feel driven to perform certain behaviors or mental acts to prevent something bad from happening, even if you know those acts might not make sense logically?

Yes. That’s exactly how it feels—driven is the right word, because it doesn’t feel like I’m calmly deciding, “Let me just double-check this.” It feels more like if I don’t do it, I’m leaving something dangerous unresolved.

So I’ll reread deployment plans, not just once but over and over, and then I’ll start cross-checking them against audit logs or permissions or access rules. And even when I’ve already confirmed it, my brain says, “But did you really confirm it, or did you just skim it?” Then I go back again. It’s the same with door locks sometimes, and even old messages—I’ll reread something I sent or approved, looking for some hidden mistake or wording that could cause a problem later.

And there’s this mental part too, where I count through the steps in my head, like I’m trying to make the sequence line up in a way that feels safe. I know that doesn’t really make logical sense. Like, counting it in my head doesn’t change the system or the lock or the message. But if I don’t do it until it feels complete, I get this spike of panic, like I’m walking away from a live wire or something.

I’ve stayed at the office for hours after everyone else has gone home because I couldn’t get to that “safe enough” feeling. I can tell myself rationally that I’ve checked it, that there’s no new information, but it doesn’t settle. It’s like stopping too early feels irresponsible, even if another part of me knows the checking has gone way past useful.
Do you experience thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or welcome—like they’re intrusive or feel foreign to you—and that cause you significant distress?

Yes. Very much so. That’s actually probably the most upsetting part, because the thoughts don’t feel like something I’m choosing to think about. They just arrive, and they have this… almost emergency quality to them.

What brings me in is that I keep getting these thoughts that if I miss one setting, one access rule, one warning sign—just one thing—then something terrible could happen. Like someone could get hurt, or lose everything, or I could be responsible for some chain of consequences I should have prevented. And I know, at least part of me knows, that it’s not always rational. I can step back sometimes and say, “Okay, this is probably disproportionate,” or “You’ve already looked at this.” But emotionally it doesn’t land that way. It hits me like I’m personally responsible, like if I move on before I’m completely certain, I’m basically choosing to let something bad happen.

And I don’t welcome those thoughts at all. I’m not sitting there wanting to imagine disasters or wanting to feel responsible for everyone’s safety. It’s the opposite. I’ll be trying to do something normal, or finish a task, and then this thought intrudes—what if you missed something, what if there’s a hidden risk, what if later everyone can trace it back to you not catching it—and then I feel this awful pressure in my chest. It’s like the thought has more authority than it should.

So yes, they feel intrusive. They feel foreign in the sense that they don’t match what I want to be thinking about, and they cause a lot of distress. I can’t just shrug them off and move on, even when I can intellectually tell they’re probably exaggerated.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, especially around the times when these intrusive thoughts are more intense?

I’m not sure. I don’t know that I’ve really separated it out that clearly.

I mean, when the thoughts are bad, I definitely feel worn down by them—like exhausted, frustrated, kind of trapped in my own head. But I don’t know if I’d call that “hopeless” exactly, or if it’s more just… being drained from trying to get through the checking and the uncertainty. It’s hard to tell where one thing ends and another begins.

As for losing interest in things, I guess I haven’t really paid attention in that way. If I’m stuck on something, then yes, other things sort of fall away because I can’t shift my attention to them. But I don’t know if that’s the same as not enjoying them anymore. It’s more like I can’t get to the point where I’m relaxed enough to enjoy anything, if that makes sense.

So… I don’t have a clean answer. I’ve noticed I feel worse when the intrusive thoughts are more intense, but I’m not sure I’d say I’ve clearly noticed being depressed or losing interest as its own separate thing.
Have you had days where you feel down or hopeless for most of the day, even when things are going okay, not just when you're caught up in these intrusive thoughts?

I don’t think I can say that clearly, no. I mean, I’ve had bad days, definitely, where I feel kind of heavy or discouraged, but when I try to look at it closely, it usually seems tied to being worn out from the thoughts or from not being able to move on from something.

The “even when things are going okay” part is harder for me to answer. I’m not sure I’ve noticed days where everything is otherwise fine and I’m just down or hopeless most of the day for no clear reason. I may be missing it, because I tend to focus so much on whether I’m keeping things under control that I don’t always stop and label my mood separately.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not sure. I don’t have a strong memory of that happening as its own separate pattern, but I also haven’t been tracking it very carefully.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or on edge in certain situations where you might be responsible for something going wrong, even if the situation isn't particularly dangerous or high-stakes?

Yes—yes, that’s exactly the kind of situation that gets me. It doesn’t even have to be something where anyone else would say, “This is a crisis.” It can be something that looks pretty ordinary from the outside, like reviewing a setting, an access rule, some warning or permission somewhere, and suddenly my mind treats it like if I miss one small thing, the consequences could be huge.

I’ll think, what if this one setting is wrong, or what if I didn’t notice some exception, and then somehow someone gets hurt, or loses everything, or there’s this whole chain of damage that comes back to me because I should have caught it. And I can tell you, part of me does know that sounds extreme. I can sometimes see that the actual situation is not that dangerous or high-stakes in the way my body is reacting to it. But it still hits me like I’m personally responsible for preventing every possible bad outcome.

So I end up feeling very on edge, because moving on feels almost like negligence. Like if I stop checking or stop thinking through every angle, then I’m choosing to let something go wrong. I know that’s not really fair or realistic, but in the moment it feels very real, and I have a hard time just saying, “Okay, good enough,” and moving on.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent intrusive thoughts related to responsibility for preventing harm, accompanied by repetitive checking behaviors aimed at reducing distress or preventing feared outcomes. These symptoms are consistent with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), specifically characterized by obsessions related to harm and compulsive checking behaviors. The compulsions are driven by an urgent need to neutralize perceived risks, even when the patient recognizes the excessiveness of these behaviors. There is partial insight, as the patient acknowledges the irrationality of the thoughts but feels unable to resist them. No sufficient evidence was found for a major depressive episode, generalized anxiety disorder, or adjustment disorder with anxiety to warrant a primary diagnosis.
